turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on through. I saw elbow on the slip, but start wherever you want.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): It's nothing, honestly. Outside of the elbow's a little sore. I almost cancelled.
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He says nothing about a leaky roof too. He winced putting the mug down this morning.
[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): So the mug. Can you actually lift a cup, or is that what sets it off?
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): I can lift it. It just zings. Not a big deal.
[SEG0006] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Six weeks of switching his coffee to the left hand. That's not nothing.
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay, fine, about six weeks. Still, I work every day.
[SEG0008] person_1 (DOCTOR): Which arm are we talking?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. Of. I'm right-handed.
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): The slip says carpenter. You painting too, or did they mix that up?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Painting mostly. Some trim, some doors. Umm, ladders all week.
[SEG0012] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Tell him about the paint can.
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): A full can tugs more than a cup, so I switch arms. Problem solved.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): Point to the spot.
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Here, the bony knob on the outside of the right elbow. Comes and goes, err, mostly when I grip a cup or a can, and ibuprofen takes the edge off. It's mild.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any swelling, redness, or does it lock on you?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Nope. No swelling. Doesn't lock. Not red.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): Numbness or tingling in the fingers?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm. No. Fingers are fine.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): What about the neck. Any stiffness, or pain shooting down from there?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Neck's good. It's the elbow and that's it.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): Walk me through the ibuprofen. How much, how often?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Two of the 200s, so 400, when it bugs me. Couple times a day on work days. Not on my days off.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Got it. Anything you swallow every day, not just for the elbow?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm. Mizartan for the pressure. And Omprazole, twenty milligrams, mornings, for heartburn.
[SEG0026] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He skips the Mizartan on weekends. Says his pressure feels fine, so why bother.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't skip it. Maybe one weekend. It's not a whole thing.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): What strength is the Mizartan?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Err. Twenty milligrams? Or forty. I don't read the label.
[SEG0030] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The bottle on the counter says 40. I've seen it.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright, we'll leave that dose unclear. Bring the bottle next time. The Omprazole you do take every morning?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, that one I actually take. Heartburn's annoying if I miss it.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any drug allergies? Ibuprofen ever swell you up, rash, trouble breathing?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Nah. No allergies.
[SEG0035] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Oh his brother can't, wait. His brother takes Metformine for his sugar. That's Dave, not him. I mixed myself up.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, Dave's thing. I don't have sugar problems.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Brother's med, not yours. Let me feel this. Tender right on that outer bump.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Little bit. See, not bad.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Push the wrist up against my hand. Yep, that fires it. No warmth, no puffiness, and you bend and straighten all the way. Grip's decent.

[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): So this walks like lateral epicondylitis, tennis elbow. The tendon on the outside gets ticked off from rollers and cans, and lifting a cup uses that same little muscle. That's the zing.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): First instinct is a steroid shot today so Monday's porch job doesn't flare you up.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't want a needle. And the ibuprofen already helps. It's minor.
[SEG0043] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He'll climb the ladder either way. Also, uh, the parking meter out front is probably dead. Just saying.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ha, we'll be done quick. Okay, thinking again, if the ibuprofen takes the edge off and you're still working, I'm not injecting today. Scratch that plan.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): What I'll actually do is put in a physical therapy referral, and I want a counterforce brace on the forearm while you paint. Ice after work, ten minutes.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): A brace. Fine. Whatever gets me out of here.

[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stay with ibuprofen 400 milligrams with food, no more than three times a day. The Omprazole should cover your stomach. Come back in four weeks. Sooner if the fingers go numb or you can't hold a brush.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Four weeks. Yeah okay. It's really not that bad.

spec.situation: Painter or carpenter with outer elbow pain for six weeks, worse lifting a cup; takes ibuprofen; physio and brace advice; no injection yet.

traps.happens: The transcript looks like speech-to-text: drug names are sometimes spelled wrongly ('Omprazole', 'Mizartan' for telmisartan, 'Metformine'), fragments and fillers appear ('Err', 'Of.', 'Mm.', 'Umm'), numbers are sometimes digits and sometimes words.
traps.label_rule: Medicine names are recorded as written in the transcript (name) with a normalized/generic name ONLY when the true drug is certain from context (a drug 'for the pressure' written 'Mizartan' is NOT certain enough: leave generic_name empty). Fragments and fillers are never facts.

features: third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.
doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.

omissions.text: Negative finding asked and answered: no neck stiffness.
Ibuprofen use detail missing: patient does not take ibuprofen on days off.
Medication instruction detail missing: ibuprofen should be taken with food.
An initial plan for a steroid injection that day to help with Monday's porch job was discussed, but the patient declined a needle and the doctor explicitly canceled that plan.
Negative history stated: patient reports he does not have 'sugar problems' (i.e., no diabetes), clarifying the brother's diabetes/Metformin is not his.
